subtype: Stage 4: Echo chamber and dehumanising talk [Observer]
passage:
Usha: you coming to the band practice sunday? everyone misses your bad drumming
Vishal: no time for that stuff anymore
Usha: since when do you not have time for drums??
Vishal: since I woke up. that whole scene is fake. all those city types are the same
Usha: all of them? your cousin lives in the city
Vishal: you know what I mean. they're the reason everything's broken here
Usha: you said the bus fare thing was the council's fault last week
Vishal: same thing. it's always them
Usha: it's 3 a.m. why are you even awake
Vishal: watching stuff. you should too. you're so asleep
(Usha stared at the screen. Vishal used to send her silly voice notes at this hour, songs about her dog.)
Usha: I miss your dog songs
Vishal: grow up

qa.q: What time was it when Usha asked why Vishal was awake?
What might Usha be feeling when she stares at the screen?
qa.a: Usha seems sad and worried, missing the funny, gentle Vishal who used to send silly songs about her dog.

qa.q: What could Usha do next, having noticed these warning signs?
qa.a: She could keep in touch warmly without arguing, ask what has been worrying Vishal, and talk to a trusted adult or counsellor about how to help.

qa.q: How does Vishal now see people who disagree, like Usha?
qa.a: Vishal sees them as 'asleep' and childish, which pushes away friends who care.

grounding: It shows a friend noticing someone who was playful now speaking in absolutes, sneering at a whole group, blaming them for everything and staying online at night.

subtype: Stage 4: Echo chamber and dehumanising talk [Observer]
passage:
In their small town near Ludhiana, Jasleen and Rajni had been the loudest pair at every wedding. Rajni did impressions of the aunties that made even the aunties laugh.
This winter, Jasleen noticed Rajni had stopped doing impressions. She'd stopped coming to kabaddi practice too, and her phulkari lay half-finished on the charpai.
At the gurdwara langar, Rajni muttered about 'the factory lot' from the new industrial area. 'They're all thieves. They're why the town's ruined. Every single one.'
'Rajni, Pinky's husband works there.'
'Then he's part of it.'
When Jasleen stayed over, she woke at three to see Rajni's face lit blue by her phone, scrolling. In the morning Rajni barely spoke about anything except 'them'.
Jasleen lay awake, trying to remember when Rajni last laughed at something that wasn't cruel.

qa.q: What did Rajni leave half-finished on the charpai?
qa.a: Her phulkari lay half-finished on the charpai.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling as she lay awake?
qa.a: Jasleen was worried and sad, missing the old, funny Rajni and troubled by her new cruelty.

qa.q: How could Jasleen respond to the warning signs she has noticed?
qa.a: She could stay close and kind, invite Rajni back to kabaddi or embroidery, calmly disagree with blaming everyone, and seek a trusted elder's advice.

qa.q: How might Pinky's husband feel if he heard Rajni call him 'part of it'?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and unfairly judged, blamed simply for where he works.

grounding: It shows a friend noticing a once-funny friend speaking in absolutes, blaming a whole group, staying online at night and losing interest in everything else.
